myth: Papaya leaf juice cures dengue and is all you need to raise platelets.
fact: There is no specific treatment that cures dengue. Care is supportive: rest, fluids and paracetamol for fever, with medical monitoring. Warning signs (severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, restlessness, fatigue) need urgent medical care. Home remedies are not a substitute for monitoring by a doctor.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Hot water with lemon cures dengue or raises platelets, so there is no need to go to hospital.
fact: No drink cures dengue or reliably raises platelet counts. There is no specific treatment for dengue; early detection and access to proper medical care lower the risk of death from severe dengue. Anyone with warning signs (severe stomach pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, restlessness) should get medical care immediately.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Goat milk raises platelets and cures dengue.
fact: There is no specific treatment or food that cures dengue. Care is supportive with fluids, rest and paracetamol, and patients with warning signs need medical care.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Eating kiwi or pomegranate cures dengue.
fact: No fruit cures dengue. There is no specific treatment; care is supportive and medical monitoring is needed, especially if warning signs appear.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Dengue mosquitoes only breed in dirty, stagnant drain water.
fact: Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes, which breed in water collected in containers around homes, such as buckets, coolers, flower pots and tyres. Removing stored and stagnant water around the home helps prevent dengue.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Any painkiller like aspirin or ibuprofen is fine for dengue fever and body pain.
fact: For dengue, paracetamol is used for pain and fever. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and aspirin should be avoided because they can increase the risk of bleeding.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Dengue and severe dengue

myth: Drinking hot water, taking hot baths or gargling kills the coronavirus.
fact: Taking hot baths or drinking hot water does not prevent or cure COVID-19. The best protection includes vaccination, good hand hygiene and avoiding crowded, poorly ventilated places when infection is spreading.
source_title: WHO: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) advice for the public - Mythbusters

myth: Eating garlic protects you from coronavirus.
fact: Garlic is a healthy food, but there is no evidence that eating garlic protects people from COVID-19.
source_title: WHO: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) advice for the public - Mythbusters

myth: Drinking cow urine or applying cow dung prevents or cures COVID-19.
fact: There is no scientific evidence that cow urine or cow dung prevents or cures COVID-19. Approved vaccines and proper medical care are the proven protections.
source_title: WHO: COVID-19 advice for the public — Mythbusters

myth: Steam inhalation kills the coronavirus in your nose and lungs.
fact: There is no scientific evidence that steam inhalation kills the virus that causes COVID-19. It can cause burns if done carelessly.
source_title: WHO: COVID-19 advice for the public — Mythbusters

myth: 5G mobile networks spread coronavirus.
fact: Viruses cannot travel on radio waves or mobile networks. COVID-19 has spread in many countries that do not have 5G networks.
source_title: WHO: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) advice for the public - Mythbusters

myth: Drinking alcohol kills the coronavirus or protects you from it.
fact: Drinking alcohol does not protect against COVID-19 and can be dangerous. Harmful alcohol use increases the risk of health problems.
source_title: WHO: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) advice for the public - Mythbusters

myth: Coronavirus cannot spread in hot and humid weather like India's summer.
fact: COVID-19 can be transmitted in all areas, including those with hot and humid weather. Exposure to the sun or high temperatures does not prevent COVID-19.
source_title: WHO: Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) advice for the public - Mythbusters

myth: COVID-19 vaccines cause infertility or impotence.
fact: There is no evidence that any vaccine, including COVID-19 vaccines, causes fertility problems in women or men. Approved COVID-19 vaccines went through safety testing and continue to be monitored.
source_title: WHO: COVID-19 vaccines — questions and answers

myth: COVID-19 vaccines contain microchips or make your arm magnetic.
fact: Vaccines do not contain microchips or metals that make the body magnetic. Their ingredients are listed and checked by regulators.
source_title: WHO: COVID-19 vaccines — questions and answers

myth: Childhood vaccines like MMR cause autism.
fact: Available scientific data show no evidence of a link between the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine and autism. Earlier studies suggesting a link were found to be seriously flawed.

myth: Polio drops are a plot to make children infertile.
fact: Polio vaccines are safe and effective and have been given to billions of children. Vaccination is the only way to protect children from polio, which can cause lifelong paralysis. There is no evidence that polio drops cause infertility.

myth: Measles is a harmless childhood illness (mata), so children do not need the vaccine.
fact: Measles is highly contagious and can cause serious complications such as pneumonia, blindness, brain swelling and death, especially in young children. Two doses of measles vaccine are safe and effective at preventing it.

myth: The HPV (cervical cancer) vaccine makes girls infertile.
fact: HPV vaccines are safe and effective at preventing infection with the HPV types that cause most cervical cancers. Vaccinating girls before they are exposed to HPV is one of the main ways to prevent cervical cancer.

myth: Drinking cow urine cures cancer.
fact: There is no scientific evidence that cow urine cures cancer. Many cancers can be cured if detected early and treated effectively with proven treatments such as surgery, radiotherapy and medicines. Delaying proper treatment lowers the chance of cure.

myth: Turmeric (haldi) milk or raw turmeric cures cancer or COVID-19.
fact: Turmeric is a common, generally safe spice, but there is no evidence that it cures cancer or COVID-19. Many cancers can be cured with early diagnosis and proven treatment; delaying that treatment for home remedies is dangerous.

myth: Bitter gourd (karela) juice cures diabetes, so you can stop insulin or diabetes tablets.
fact: No food or juice cures diabetes. People with type 1 diabetes need insulin to survive, and many people with type 2 diabetes need medicines to control blood sugar. Diet and exercise help but are not a replacement for prescribed treatment. Never stop insulin or tablets without talking to your doctor.

myth: Soaked methi (fenugreek) seeds or cinnamon cure diabetes permanently.
fact: A healthy diet, regular physical activity and a healthy weight help manage type 2 diabetes, but no single food cures it. Treatment, regular testing and medicines when prescribed are needed to avoid complications such as heart attack, kidney failure and blindness.

myth: Diabetes is caused only by eating too much sugar or sweets.
fact: Type 2 diabetes is linked mainly to excess body weight and physical inactivity, along with genetics; type 1 diabetes is not caused by diet. Sugary foods and drinks can contribute through weight gain, but they are not the only cause.

myth: Once blood pressure is normal, or if you eat garlic or drink lauki juice, you can stop BP tablets.
fact: High blood pressure is usually a long-term condition. Medicines keep it controlled, and stopping them without medical advice can let blood pressure rise again, raising the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney damage. Lifestyle changes help but should be added to, not replace, prescribed treatment.

myth: Rock salt (sendha namak) or pink salt is safe in any amount for people with high BP.
fact: All types of salt contain sodium. Eating too much sodium raises blood pressure. WHO recommends adults eat less than 5 g of salt a day.

myth: Putting onion slices in your socks or under your feet draws out fever.
fact: There is no scientific evidence that onions placed on the body reduce fever. Fever can signal infections such as dengue, malaria or typhoid; a high or lasting fever should be checked by a doctor.
source_title: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Government of India

myth: Keeping an onion in your pocket prevents heatstroke.
fact: There is no evidence that carrying an onion prevents heatstroke. Drinking enough water, avoiding the sun in the hottest hours, and wearing light clothing help prevent heat illness. Heatstroke is an emergency that needs immediate medical care.
source_title: National Centre for Disease Control, Government of India

myth: Antibiotics cure colds, flu and viral fever.
fact: Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses such as those causing colds and flu. Misusing antibiotics drives antimicrobial resistance, which makes infections harder to treat. Take antibiotics only when prescribed.

myth: TB is hereditary or incurable.
fact: Tuberculosis is caused by bacteria that spread through the air when people with TB cough. It is preventable and curable with a full course of medicines.

myth: You can stop TB medicines once you feel better.
fact: TB is curable with a full course of medicines, usually lasting months. Stopping early can make the illness return and can lead to drug-resistant TB, which is much harder to treat.

myth: After a dog bite, applying chilli, turmeric or oil to the wound is enough; no injection needed.
fact: Rabies is almost always fatal once symptoms appear, but it is preventable. After a bite, immediately wash the wound with soap and water for about 15 minutes and get post-exposure vaccination (and immunoglobulin if advised) at a health facility as soon as possible.

myth: For snakebite, suck out the poison, tie a tight rope above the bite, or take the person to a faith healer.
fact: Snakebite is a medical emergency. Keep the person calm and still and take them to a hospital quickly; antivenom is the effective treatment. Traditional methods such as cutting, sucking or tight tourniquets can cause harm and waste time.

myth: HIV spreads by touching, hugging, sharing food or mosquito bites.
fact: HIV spreads through certain body fluids such as blood, breast milk, semen and vaginal fluids. It is not spread by everyday contact such as hugging, shaking hands or sharing food. Effective treatment lets people with HIV live long, healthy lives.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: HIV and AIDS

myth: Neem leaf smoke or giloy alone cures malaria; no test or medicine needed.
fact: Malaria is preventable and curable, but it needs to be confirmed by a test and treated with effective antimalarial medicines. Delayed treatment can make malaria severe and life-threatening.

myth: A child with diarrhoea should be given less water and food so the loose motions stop.
fact: Diarrhoea is dangerous mainly because of dehydration. Children with diarrhoea should get oral rehydration solution (ORS) and zinc and continue to be fed. Seek care if the child cannot drink, has blood in stool or seems very sick.

myth: The first yellow breast milk (colostrum) is bad and should be thrown away; give the newborn honey or ghutti instead.
fact: Colostrum, the first milk, is the perfect food for a newborn. WHO recommends starting breastfeeding within the first hour after birth and giving only breast milk, with no other foods or drinks, for the first six months.
source_title: WHO fact sheet: Infant and young child feeding

myth: Making a person smell a shoe or onion stops an epileptic fit; epilepsy is caused by evil spirits.
fact: Epilepsy is a non-communicable brain condition, not caused by spirits. Up to 70% of people with epilepsy could live seizure-free with appropriate medicines. Smelling shoes or onions does not stop a seizure.

myth: Depression is just weakness or laziness, not a real illness.
fact: Depression is a common mental disorder, not a weakness. Effective treatments exist, including psychological treatment and, in some cases, medicines.

myth: Hepatitis B spreads by eating together or sharing utensils.
fact: Hepatitis B spreads through blood and body fluids, including from mother to baby at birth, unsafe injections and unprotected sex. It is not spread by sharing food or utensils. A safe and effective vaccine prevents it.

myth: Chewing tobacco, gutka or smoking after meals helps digestion and relieves stress.
fact: All forms of tobacco are harmful. Tobacco kills up to half of its users who do not quit, and smokeless tobacco causes cancers of the mouth and throat.

myth: Conjunctivitis (eye flu) spreads just by looking into an infected person's eyes.
fact: Conjunctivitis does not spread by looking at someone's eyes. It spreads through contact with eye discharge, for example via hands, towels or shared items. Washing hands and not sharing towels helps prevent it.
source_title: National Centre for Disease Control, Government of India
